text: Good afternoon. This is April Chandler calling to order the Legislative Audit and Policy Committee meeting for April 25th, 2024. We would normally begin with public comment, but seeing none, we'll move on. We are absolutely delighted today to welcome our Loudon delegation and to join us in this Legislative Audit and Policy Committee meeting, as well as the many members of the school board.

We all appreciate having the opportunity to hear directly from each of you about the successes and challenges of the recent session and to learn more about the bills that we work together to champion in support of the students and staff of Loudoun County Public Schools.

Today, we'll start with Chair Mansfield and Dr. Spence offering some brief comments before we'll hear from each important member of our delegation. And I would also like to take a moment to recognize our school board members who are in attendance.
You'll see there's Chair Mansfield, Vice Chair Estreffi, Ms. Chernoff, Dr. Deans, Dr. Rasheed, and of course, Ms. Donahue. Oh, right, Ms. Donahue?

Yep. Right. Thank you for taking this time to join us today, school board members. And please take the opportunity to note your questions, as we will have some time at the end of the meeting to ask questions of our esteemed delegation.

And before I hand over the microphone to Chair Mansfield, I would like to say welcome back, Delegate Reeser, and say thank you for all of your hard work as a delegate and also as past chair of this committee. Delegate Reeser worked tirelessly to develop our Loudoun County School Board legislative program.

some of which will be highlighted today. And congratulations also, Delia Reeser, on the passage of Adams Law. This is so important to our shared Algonquian community, and we also appreciate your work as the only Loudoun member of the K-12 subcommittee.

Now, I'll hand the microphone over to Chair Mansfield. Thank you, Chair Chandler. Good afternoon to all of you. Thank you so much for being here, and thank you all so much for your support of Loudoun County Public Schools. Our partnership with our state delegation is so critically important to our success as a school division, so thank you for being our advocates in Richmond.

I want to give a huge thank you to Senator Subranayam for coming and for your advocacy for our students while you served on the K-12 subcommittee in the House last year. We appreciate you carrying SB 187, a Loudoun County School Board priority, that would have DOE develop a plan for revised special education staffing requirement.

That bill that has been rolled into Senator Lucas's large omnibus and is still awaiting for the governor's action. And I'm hoping that we will see movement as a result of your efforts. Thank you. And to Delegate Higgins, who was not all that long ago served in this very room as a school board member.

Got a little picture. I think he's right there. Come see you later. Only yesterday. I thank you for your continued interest in public education and for bringing forward legislation this year related to school connected overdoses. We also appreciate your consideration of the bill's expansion to include community-wide reporting of overdoses. We can all agree that opioid access in our community is a significant issue that requires a collaborative, intentional response. We know

that most juvenile overdoses in Loudoun County do not happen in our schools, which means that without expanded community-wide reporting, our parents and community would likely not know about them. And lastly, a special thank you to Delegate Martinez, who tirelessly advocated for the literacy audit bill. HB 211 would have required audits of education preparation programs. While the bill was continued to 2025, I'm confident that with help from our delegation in the community, we can get that passed next year. And now I would like to hand the mic over to our superintendent, Dr. Aaron

Spence. Thank you, Madam Chair. And Ms. Chandler, thank you as well. And again, I would express the same thing on behalf of the administration, how pleased we are to be able to be with our delegation this afternoon in conversation about the ongoing session. And I would like to start by specifically thanking Delegate Trina Vassanen and Senator Perry for being great budget patrons and advocates for one of our top priorities, which was bringing funding and authorization for a recovery school of Loudoun County. And I'm very pleased and want to praise your staff from both offices as you were

working that funding through the legislature. Just a quick update in terms of where we are based on our understanding of that funding. We are first and foremost extremely grateful for the consideration and want to be clear in here with the delegation that the funding we received is going to allow us to support a planning year in 24-25. So we're not going to be able to open a building with that funding, but what we will be able to do is further develop a very comprehensive program to include a curriculum, identified resource materials, figure out the scheduling and other logistics to include the space where we would put the building.

So we look forward to a productive planning year and keeping our delegation informed both as required in the funding mechanism, but also just through our conversations. And we certainly look forward to continuing to partner with the Loudoun County delegation to keep this priority and need at the forefront of our continued work together.

Also, if you'll indulge me, I'd like to just talk a little bit about our priorities as you head towards the budget special session. And here are a few things that we're thinking about. First and foremost, we are really hopeful that we can quickly get to a resolution on the budget, that the General Assembly and the governor can quickly get to a resolution on the budget.

As you know, that does impact our funding and our planning as we head into the new school year. and so we're hopeful for productive conversations there. One area that the governor and General Assembly both have shown a commitment to is teacher salaries, and both budget proposals provided funding for teachers at a 3% pay increase next year.

That is sorely needed for the division to continue to recruit and retain the highest caliber teachers in the state. In contrast, restoration of payments in lieu of the grocery sales tax removal is very important to LCPS, although I don't speak for them directly, know that we have also heard it's important to our Board of Supervisors. As a reminder, the state did eliminate the sales tax on grocery and personal hygiene products effective January 1st, 2023, and concurrent to that, recognizing the negative impact this would have on schools, the state also committed to providing payments in lieu of the sales tax that would have been collected had it not been eliminated. The General Assembly budget

included funding to continue the payments, those in lieu payments, and we're very grateful for that and grateful for our delegation support but the governor's budget does not include that and we want to advocate for the inclusion of that in the budget an estimated 9.6 million dollars of state funding is in jeopardy and if it's not received lcps would need to engage in discussions with the county to fill that gap in our budget so with those as our as our budget priorities as you head into the the next session or the special session we would just say again thank you for all of your work on behalf of Loudoun County Public Schools and your willingness to remain

in constant contact with us as we've talked about the various issues that we've been facing together. And with that, Ms. Chandler, I'll turn it back to you. Thank you, Dr. Spence. I'm happy to start the program off with Senator Perry. Good afternoon to y'all. I just want to say thank you first and foremost to everyone for having us all here today. I think I can speak on behalf of the delegation and the wonderful people that I have the privilege to serve with. I'm going to start out by talking just a little bit about the budget that came out of the General Assembly this year because I think the budget that came out of the General Assembly budget, we first and foremost

describe it as a pro-education budget. And it was incredibly important to those of us who passed that budget that that's exactly what it was. And so I just want to talk real briefly about what it is that that budget does. That budget, compared to the governor's proposed budget, the budget that was passed out by the General Assembly includes an additional $1.2 billion for public schools.

This is an unprecedented level of investment in public schools, and I think that demonstrates the importance to this delegation of public schools, what it is that our public schools provide to us as a community and to us as a country and to us as our democracy. In our budget, that includes for Loudoun County Public Schools in particular, a total of $57 million.

That's $4 million for low-income students, $700 per pupil, $5 million for English language learners or ELL students, 60 new ELL instructors, $20.4 million for teacher and staff salaries, including the 3% salary increase with a four-year goal to bring salaries to the national average and keep them there.

Virginia, as we learned in the JLARC study, has fallen behind surrounding states and is, in my opinion, far behind where it is that we need to be to support our students, support our staff, and the folks who are relying and depending on us to do the right thing. As many of you all know, the General Assembly rejected all 233 of the governor's amendments and called a May 13th special session.

We will be down there to try to negotiate the budget and come to some resolution. I do know that Latin County Public Schools, along with all localities and counties and towns and cities in the state, are depending on us to come to a resolution and to deliver for the people, and I know that that is important to each and every one of us here on this delegation.

As was mentioned, I was privileged this year and am incredibly proud to have been able to carry the budget amendment. Superintendent Spence approached me prior to session about carrying that recovery school budget amendment.

my background is as a prosecutor. I did a lot with kids, but I also served on our drug court here in Loudoun County. So being able to deliver on the opioid crisis and the opioid crisis as it particularly impacts the youngest amongst us is of particular importance to me. I want to thank Delegate Srinivasan for carrying the House version of it. That money was included in the budget this year. The conference budget included a total of $750,000 for the Loudoun County Recovery School, $500,000 in the first year to cover startup costs with an additional $250,000 in the second year for operational costs. I don't anticipate that that will get removed out of any kind of a

negotiated budget. I expect that that will be included in the budget, and we're very privileged to be able to deliver on that. Obviously, the issue of the opioid crisis has been a very important topic here in Loudoun County, as it should be, and across all of Northern Virginia. Again, I think we owe it to our students, to our children here, to do everything we can to take care of them, And I think providing for them some sort of a recovery school where they can go and be away from those who know recovery people, places, and things that can trigger relapses, that can trigger an inability to continue on with their education, which is probably the most important thing for those kids.

I know there's a lot of discussion around notification and this, that, and the other, and I'm happy to answer any questions about any of that in my particular position on it. But for right now, I'm just pleased to be able to deliver that money to Loudoun County and to the people and folks who are delivering on it. I do want to talk about, I did co-patron the bill that, the Senate bill that came out related to opioid overdoses, and I also co-patroned an additional bill that authorized all counties and cities to enact an additional sales and use tax to support schools if it was approved by a voter referendum.

That rate should not exceed 1%. That bill was vetoed by the governor, but it is, I think, an additional bill that will come back before the General Assembly as a way for schools across the country to implement their own localities decide whether or not they think that, hey, some additional local funding would be helpful to us in funding our public schools. So that continues to be a priority for the General Assembly. Another bill that I signed onto and co-sponsored had to do with providing free meals for kids in public schools who are struggling, kids who, you know, don't have meals,

don't have a free meal for them to have the state kick in and provide money so that no kid goes to school and is hungry there that will continue to be a priority for us in the General Assembly and is a bill that I believe the governor did sign and it will go into law. I'm not going to continue to talk. There are some other bills that some of my friends and colleagues have carried and so I am though happy to continue to partner with each and every one of you. I made a pledge to not be part-time legislator, but to be a full-time legislator, which we all actually do. But that means that I intend to work on introducing legislation all year long, getting legislation

drafted and having it be good legislation. So please don't wait until November to talk to me. I'm here now. I'll be here tomorrow and the next day and the next day here, either here or in Richmond. But reach out and let me know what it is that I can do for you, what it is we can do for you. I think I speak for all of us when I say we're here to serve. I'm going to turn this over to my colleague and the other senator from Loudoun County, Senator Suha Subramaniam.

Thank you, Madam Chair, and everyone here on the school board for having us today. And thank you, Senator Perry, for your comments. I just want to build on what Senator Perry covered on the budget first, and I think highlight a few differences.

I, for instance, really applaud the initiative of the General Assembly and the governor for making a commitment to increase funding for teachers. I think the governor's proposal, though, funds it for the first year at 1%, and then the second year at 2%.

And so he's saying 3%, but ours actually does it at 3% for the next two years. So there's little differences in the budget that we're going to be fighting for as we negotiate this. that I think in the end reflects the values that I know many of you and I certainly have, which is fully fund our schools, pay our teachers, do what's best for our students.

Senator Perry mentioned the investment, the commitment we're making to schools, and we wanted to make sure that Loudoun County schools especially get the resources that they need. Another thing that the governor's budget does not do that I think we do a better job of in the General Assembly's budget is the funding needs for special education as well as additional literacy support.

I think those are things that when we think about fully funding schools again, we have to fully fund all the programs and make sure all the kids are taken care of and not just keeping the lights on. And so part of, I went to this session and carried legislation, SB 187, that got rolled into Senator Lucas's an omnibus bill on making sure that we have the staffing requirements for special education, students with special needs.

And we sent that bill to the governor. He came back with some amendments. I'm happy to talk in more detail later about those amendments. But the long story short is we rejected those amendments. We hope he'll sign the bill that we put forward because I think in the end, this was based on Jay Lark's very extensive study on the issue, and I'd say the number one thing when I was talking to folks over the past couple years I came up, when I came to education, was really the special education and sort of the deficiencies we have and the needs that every level of government needs to help support that initiative.

And so we're really looking forward to hopefully getting the governor to sign this bill as is and making sure that we can shore up special across the Commonwealth and especially here in Loudoun. - Senator Perry mentioned free school lunches, that work group I hope will move forward with good recommendations to implement that.

I know some initiatives were meant for just COVID times, but I think some initiatives proved to be very successful. And so we should learn from what really worked and what really helped kids during COVID and make that permanent. And I think that's one example of something that should. And the final thing is, Senator Perry just talked about how legislation should happen all year round.

one of the best bills I got this session actually was a very last minute bill SB 707 and it's from a group of middle school kids who really wanted to start a HOSA chapter in their middle school a formal middle school and unfortunately because of the the rules and regulations in Virginia they were told that they were not allowed to start one and I heard from several other schools and kids from those schools as well that they wanted to start these career and technical education clubs whether it was a health club like HOSA or another technical education club but they needed to have the required class to do it but other states don't require that

and so these students actually helped me write the bill themselves talking to 7th and 8th graders and then they came and testified for the committee and even the Department of Education had someone go up there and oppose the bill but they were able to out-debate the Department of Education and then what I loved was we got the bill passed and we even had them testify remotely.

About seven or eight kids lined up and testified on Zoom in front of the Education Committee, and Delegate Reeser was there to see that. And we got this bill before the governor, and the Department of Education came down with suggestions that would essentially kill the bill.

And I got that email at 9 a.m., and by 5 p.m., the governor had backed down and said, we'll sign the bill, don't worry about it, because kids across the state were reaching out to the governor's office, telling them that we want to make sure that this bill gets signed as is and sure enough the bill got signed and so I think if we get more of our students and not just students but you know faculty and you all supporting these types of initiatives that's the best way legislation happens is when it comes from the community and I look at us as just a conduit for that so thank you for supporting that bill and I know the kids are really excited and I think we're all invited to the launch of their HOSA chapter this fall too so I thank you

for being a part of that thank you senator Perry and Senator Subramaniam we're so grateful for those updates and we'll move on to the house delegation delegate Higgins you have the floor thank you very much it's a wonderful opportunity to be here again with you all I need to correct the record on one thing I when I was on the school board we didn't meet in this building we met over in Leesburg in what is now the I think it's adult senior center or something on north street but while i was on the board we did uh vote for this building that's a whole nother

story that i won't bother you with tonight this afternoon um you know as we all know uh and i've had the opportunity and been blessed to be able to sit at the school board level and the board of supervisors level and now in the house of delegates i kind of seen this thing from a lot of different directions um i will say that in in the end uh when you get to the budget it's a series of choices, and nobody gets everything that they want, although you should fight for the priorities that you think are important. And so, you know, I've seen, I think now, three iterations

of the budget, one that the governor brought, one that the House brought, one that the Senate brought back to the House after they talked. And so we've had three budgets, and we're going to get ready to have our our fourth and I think some of these priorities need to be hammered out you can't have everything you want when you have choices I mean we have a budget that came back out of the joint committee of the house and senate with a two and a half billion dollar tax increase and the governor isn't ready to sign that and has indicated he will not so I'm encouraged that the rhetoric

from both parties has ceased going into these discussions, serious discussions about the budget, and I hope that people will get serious about getting to some place that is the right place to be. You know, one of the problems that I had when we go to the budget and the priorities that people set, and I've always supported teacher pay, go back and watch all the votes, maybe not all that everybody wanted, but we've always supported increases in teacher pay.

My wife is a teacher, so I hear it from both sides. Having said that, you know, in the budget that we dealt with initially from the House and Senate, while there was increases in the teacher's pay, some of the things that nobody talks about that were cut out of that budget include $350 million that were earmarked for teachers' pensions, and that's big money.

And maybe I have a problem with things like that, having been a Taft-Hartley trustee, But when you start messing around with pension money, you create things that you can't necessarily catch up with. The state of New Jersey and the state of Illinois has both played with public pension money, and you can see the situation they got into financially.

So Virginia doesn't want to be like that. Virginia's pension plan is funded at 80%, which is good, but that's not real good. It should be funded more like 90%, and we shouldn't be pulling money out of the pension to spend it elsewhere. Another thing that was near and dear to my heart that got cut out of that budget was $8 million in funding for school resource officers.

When I ran for state senate in 2019, every person in this county ran for school resource officers and increased funding for them. And we've had at least two iterations of cutting that by, I think, a total of $17 or $18 million.

So, you know, when we talk about safety of our schools and safety of our children, I think school resource officers play a big part in that. So right now, it'll be interesting to see what happens with the discussions on the budget. I don't think, and correct me if I'm wrong, I don't think any of the delegation from Loudoun is part of the committees that are meeting, although we have communications with some of those individuals.

So we look forward to giving them input and talking about, you know, what kind of things we need to hear from you all that need to be funded. I was also a co-sponsor on the recovery school. I think that's a great opportunity for Loudoun, particularly in the face of the opioid situation that we've been facing.
I have to say that I was disappointed in how the opioid thing notification was ultimately handled. There were four different persons, Democrat and Republican, that brought forth those bills.

All four of them included the 24-hour notification. Somehow it got stripped out in committee, and then when the governor put it back, all he did was put back in what was the original request of the four legislators that put them in, and that was voted down in the House, that amendment.

So I don't quite understand that. Somebody upstairs had, I guess, made that decision. They weren't going to support that. But my concern is that parents need to know what's going on in the schools, need to know about overdoses and other things. In the situation we have today with social media, the only people that won't know about the overdoses will be the parents because everybody else will be talking about it in social media.

So they need to be notified. And unfortunately, that didn't happen. But I have a feeling we'll see it again next year. So we'll talk about that then. Let me think what else I want to talk about here for a minute. We'll have to see what comes out of the budget negotiations, and hopefully things will be in the right area for school funding and adequately.

I know the other thing I want to talk about. There was a bill in the House that was going to mandate getting all of our school systems up to the average, I think it was Bill HB 187, that was going to mean that all of our schools in Virginia over a period of time were going to have to get up to the average of, I believe, across the country, average competition of teachers, average teacher salary.

And while we want to get teacher salaries up, that mandate on the part of many of our schools in rural areas would have put a mandate on them that they couldn't have dealt with. So the governor brought that back with an amendment saying that we would study that every year and make sure that we, you know, consider that in our deliberations about school teacher salaries, which was not supported in the House. And I don't understand why that wasn't supported, but it wasn't. So hopefully we can get something like that passed again next year as well. I have enjoyed working with

my friends from Northern Virginia. We work together on a lot of different issues, not just school issues, but other issues, and so I think it's great that whatever partisan differences get set aside on those issues and we can work seriously together, and I appreciate that, and I do appreciate the work that you all do. I know about the work that you all do, and I would love to hear from you about the things that you want us to work on, so thank you for the opportunity to be here and listen today.

Thank you, Delegate Higgins. Delegate Reeser, the floor is yours. Thank you, Madam Chair. It's really nice to say that. Well, it's really good to be back here with you all. It feels a little bit like coming home. So thank you for continuing to have this road from Richmond for our delegation to come and talk with you and report back to you everything we've been able to do.

Some of you know my district runs through all of eastern Loudoun County. It's 100% in Loudoun. And I think this is the first year that your Loudoun delegation, I know some of the senators have bigger districts, but you have your very own dedicated delegates in your delegation.

And it's nice to have a full delegation. It's been really wonderful to partner with everyone, both in the other chamber and across our chamber, to be able to deliver for Loudoun County. As you know, the decisions that we make don't impact just our district. just as yours impact the entire school division and the school district ours also impact all of the commonwealth but I think it's fair for me to say on behalf of my colleagues and I that we worked really hard to continue to move Virginia forward with the priorities of taking care of Loudoun's families the businesses the the students the workforce here and keeping that top of mind

is is what was kind of my my guiding principle in in the work that I did I was able to serve on three committees this year. I was on courts of justice, education, the K-12 subcommittee, as Chair Chandler said, and on county cities and towns, which all tapped into my professional experience and my time working here on the school board. And I think that the depth of experience from having been here for four years is probably what enabled me to really dig in on the issues that came up in the K-12 subcommittee, which I believe, my staff tells me, had the most number of bills of any subcommittee.

So it was a lot of work. We started at 7.30 on Tuesday mornings, and sometimes we met twice on Tuesday. And it was really one of the highlights was having the Loudoun students come and speak on Senator Supermanian's bill. They did remember coming to speak to our previous board here, and they did a really good job, I think, representing Loudoun and using their student voices, which I know is something that this school division has championed for many, many years since before I was able to serve on the board and I'm sure for long after.

Those student voices make a really big difference, and we appreciate the excellent education that you have equipped them with that allowed them to represent the division so well and to be so successful. As Senator Subramaniam said, even in having something pass that maybe the state's Department of Education initially thought wasn't a good idea.

So in prioritizing education, as my colleagues talked about, we did prioritize teacher pay. I think that getting to at least the national average is a floor and not a ceiling. Closing the funding gap for our students who have the most need, the ELL students, the economically disadvantaged, those that are at risk because they have special needs. Those are things that we all worked on and your board continues to work on. And I think we know as educators that helping those students allows our professionals, our educators and our staff to then also be able to help students who don't have special needs or are at risk because when there's

proper funding it allows for proper staffing ratios and other supports that then frees up educators to help everyone in their classroom. So I hope that the new budget or the future budgets will continue to prioritize those needs because I think that helps every student and all of our families. I'd also like to talk a little bit about what we were able to prevent not just what we were able to champion. I believe that in divided government, you do have to make compromises, and it is the General Assembly's position that giving tax breaks to the wealthiest and shifting the economic burden to those who have the most need and are the most vulnerable Virginians is

not the way that Virginia should move forward. So I believe that the General Assembly's approach to taking the governor's proposed tax on digital services and making it, I think we call it modernizing the tax code, making it a little bit more fair so that it's not just individuals like you and I who are paying taxes on digital services, but also including companies and corporations in that will give us more of the income that we need to fund some of these priorities that we've all talked about here today.

And it's my hope that with the budget that comes back in May that we're able to support the priorities we talked about by shifting some of the proposed tax burdens across to businesses and not just those of us who already have a lot of burden to bear.

So some of the bills that I was able to work on also supported these priorities I'm talking about. In terms of supporting families and workforce, one of my favorite bills was what my staff called the Babies in Buildings Bill. It allows for businesses to provide child daycare, which currently is not something that's allowed. It'll be a local option, so no one has to do it, but if you should choose to do that, you'll possibly be able to also provide child care in buildings where people work. This helps families, it helps working moms, it helps working dads, but it also helps businesses

that have empty commercial space. And it was something that I heard from different chambers of commerce, as well as the Northern Virginia Chamber of Commerce, as a helpful step forward to filling up some of the space that continues to sit empty since the pandemic caused some shifts in spaces being occupied in buildings, and more people are still continuing to work hybrid as they make their work-life balance.

Another one of the bills that Senator Perry and I got to co-patron, well, chief patron across the different chambers, raises the statutory cap on court-appointed counsel. And while I'm mentioning these bills, and they may not seem to touch on education specifically, I think they touch to some of the bigger things that our community needs.

Our court-appointed counsel provides constitutional protections, which ultimately comes back to help every single one of us, just as workforce development does. I had about 11 bills that we filed initially.

Nine of them passed both chambers, and seven of them were passed into law. Of those, all of them had bipartisan support, and many of them were unanimously supported by both chambers. And I mention this because I think it's important for you to know that despite how things seem sometimes on the outside, we really do try to collaborate and pass legislation that works for the Commonwealth for the good.

I think that it is our duty and our responsibility both to our local government and all of the folks that elected us to continue to try to push forward things that people can agree on. And it's my hope that the change in that climate and that attitude trickles down to how local boards are treated as well.

One last thing I'll talk about, well, two last things I'll talk about. As one of you mentioned, I was able to work with the Oaks family to bring forward and have successfully passed some legislation that you will have to work on writing a policy for implementing hazing prevention instruction.

I know that at one point, the school division wanted to add that instruction for athletic directors, and perhaps that's something we could think about taking back in passing, although I have heard that the Senate has indicated that they would look less favorably next year on education bills that put more requirements for school divisions to implement, and I think it's inherently obvious why, but if that is something that Loudoun County Public Schools and the Loudoun County Public Schools School Board decide you would like to have championed it's certainly something that we can take back and and work on and expanding that

instruction to athletic directors but I think certainly there's nothing that would prevent your athletic directors from participating when the students are receiving the instruction so it may be something that you just choose to do without having a state mandate to do it. And the last thing I'll touch on is some work that I was able to do with delegate Laura Jane Cohen who was a school board member in Fairfax. I talked in the beginning about priorities that we had for the Commonwealth, and I talked about taking care of our workers, being one of the priorities, and taking care of the safety of our students was another one of the priorities. With gun-related

deaths being a major threat for students and being a number one killer of students, one of the things that we talked about doing was how we could better inform families about existing laws. So not passing more law, but just informing them about what's already required in terms of safe storage of weapons. We both had that bill. We wanted school divisions to send a notification to parents, making it really transparent and obvious for them what their existing duties are.

We decided to just roll our bills into one. Frankly, hers was more well-written, so I became a chief co-sponsor of her bill, and that bill was amended to the point where she didn't feel like it, my mistake. Her bill was actually vetoed, so we weren't even able to consider accepting the amendment.

So hopefully we'll be able to bring that back next year and see if we can champion that along with any other bills that you all decide as a committee to put together. Thank you. Thank you, Delegate Reeser. Delegate Srinivasan, the floor is yours. Thank you, Madam Chair.

Thanks for having me. Thanks for what all you do. This was an extraordinary opportunity to work in the General Assembly with a fellow delegation and across the aisle. A couple of bills that relates to education that I was able to work on and pass, that I worked with your teams, House Bill 919, that's an MOU on mental health services to enable partnerships with virtual service providers.

Health is what brought me to politics, so I'm in the Health and Human Services Committee, So this will enable more virtual mental health services, very important, particularly post-COVID, and also the administration has a big initiative, RightHelpRightNow, which I'm a big fan of.

So I was very proud to work on this bill, get it passed and get it signed. So hopefully this is another tool in the toolkit to offer these services. There are multiple companies that can join. This will obviously, it's permissive, and it also will follow your standards.

what you will negotiate. So I was happy to do that. The second one, the budget amendment that Senator Perry talked about, I was happy to carry that on the House side. It was actually $1.5 million. Then I realized it is split with Virginia Beach, $750.

And I said, wow, Superman and Spence is from Virginia Beach. So, you know, it's perfectly fine. So that's for Zone 4 here.
